register.text: A three-year IMF arrangement of SDR 1.369 billion, about US$1.9 billion, in support of Bolivia’s economic programme. The Banco Central de Bolivia records the first disbursement, SDR 156.1 million, on 6 October 2026. It stands behind the coordinated support of the World Bank, the IDB and CAF, on which public spending across the seven standards depends.

Executed by the Empresa Nacional de Electricidad (ENDE), it adds clean generation to the energy standard.

dispatches.label: 16 Nov 2026
dispatches.author: steward
dispatches.title: World Bank approves US$500 million to steady Bolivia’s public finances
dispatches.summary: On 12 November 2026 the World Bank Group approved US$500 million of general budget support for Bolivia, the first of two planned operations, alongside an IMF arrangement and support from the IDB and CAF.
body: On 12 November 2026 the World Bank Group approved US$500 million to support fiscal sustainability and job creation in Bolivia. It is general budget support for a period of adjustment, when the government needs liquidity while its measures take effect, and it is the first of a series of two planned operations.

The World Bank Group is the lender. Its release does not state the lending arm, the tenor or the rate. The financing is part of a coordinated package of international support with the IMF, the Inter-American Development Bank and CAF. The IMF Executive Board approved a 36-month Extended Fund Facility arrangement for Bolivia on 2 October 2026: SDR 1.369 billion, about US$1.9 billion, with SDR 156 million, about US$214 million, available at once.

The money is not tied to one project. It backs two sets of measures the government has already adopted: stronger public finances with protection for poor and vulnerable households; and an economy more open to private investment, through a modern framework for fintech providers, more flexible credit requirements, wider access to finance, easier agricultural exports and greater private participation in electricity.

Of the seven standards, it moves livelihood most directly, through jobs, credit and farm exports. Private participation in electricity bears on energy. The protection of poor and vulnerable households is meant to shield them while the public finances are put right.

Could it work elsewhere? The design, liquidity released against reforms already taken and coordinated across the IMF and the development banks, could serve another nation that must steady its budget before it can borrow on markets again, such as Malawi. The second operation in the series will show whether Bolivia keeps the reforms in place.
